title: Bengal Famine Changed South Asian DNA

cards.prompt: The Bengal famine happened in the year ____.
Which diseases caused massive loss of life in the famine?
Explain like I'm 10: how did the famine change people's bodies?
cards.answer: Their bodies went into survival mode and needed fewer calories. Later when food was plentiful, they stored fat easily, which raised the risk of type 2 diabetes. These changes were passed on to children.

cards.prompt: At what age do South Asians develop type 2 diabetes risk compared to Europeans?
cards.answer: South Asians by age 25, Europeans by age 40.

cards.prompt: The famine was purely natural and not man-made.
cards.answer: It was man-made: British colonial blocked food supply to civilians, prioritizing military needs.

cards.prompt: Why did people who stored more fat survive better during the famine?
cards.answer: They had energy reserves to survive starvation.
Blockade led to famine, bodies adapted, and the adaptation was inherited.

cards.prompt: A South Asian friend asks why they should check diabetes risk earlier than a European friend. Explain using the famine.
cards.answer: The famine altered genes toward survival mode with easy fat storage; inherited, this raises type 2 diabetes risk earlier.

cards.prompt: What does "enough threshold lowered" mean for the body after famine?
options: It needs fewer calories and stores excess as fat easily
cards.answer: The body needs less food and stores extra as fat easily.
